summary: This draft standard describes Post Office Protocol version 3, a simple way for a mail client to fetch email from a mail server. It revises RFC 1225 and was replaced by RFC 1725.

eli5.summary: Email waits for you on a server. POP3 is the way a mail program says, let me pick up what is waiting for me.

questions: how does post office protocol work
what are the pop3 session states
subtitle: A simple protocol for a mail client to pick up and delete the mail waiting for it on a server.

tldr.problem: Small workstations often cannot run a full mail transport system or stay connected all the time, yet their users still need to read their mail.
tldr.mechanism: A server host holds the mail in a maildrop. The client opens a TCP connection to port 110, logs in, lists, retrieves and marks messages, and the server deletes the marked ones when the session ends.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1460 revises RFC 1225 and was itself replaced by RFC 1725, so it is no longer the current POP3 definition.

today: RFC 1460 was a Draft Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 1725, so read that document for the later POP3 definition. It itself revised RFC 1225.

sections.title: Why POP3 Exists
sections.content:
On smaller nodes it is often impractical to maintain a message transport system (MTS). A workstation may lack the cycles or disk space to keep an SMTP server and a local delivery system running, and a personal computer may not be connected to the network for long. So a node that can run an MTS offers a maildrop service. The Post Office Protocol, Version 3 (POP3) lets a workstation dynamically access a maildrop on a server host, usually to retrieve mail the server is holding for it.

This memo is a revision of RFC 1225. It removes the RPOP facility, adds the optional APOP facility, fixes a typo about how LAST and RSET interact, and adds section numbers and acknowledgements.
sections.eli5: A tiny computer cannot stay on all day to catch mail. So a bigger computer keeps the mail safe, and POP3 lets the small one fetch it later.

sections.title: Basic Operation and Session States
sections.content:
The server listens on TCP port 110. After a client connects, the server sends a greeting, and then they trade commands and responses. A command is a keyword with an optional argument, ended by a CRLF pair. A response starts with a success indicator, either +OK or -ERR.

Some responses are multi-line. After the first line, further lines follow, and a final line holding only a period ends the response, so the whole thing ends with the five octets CRLF.CRLF. A line that begins with a period is byte-stuffed by adding another period in front, and the client strips it.

A session moves through three states. It starts in AUTHORIZATION, where the client identifies itself. After the server locks the maildrop, it enters TRANSACTION, where the client issues commands. When the client sends QUIT, it enters UPDATE, where the server releases its resources and says goodbye. Then the TCP connection closes.
sections.eli5: A visit has three parts: show your ID at the door, pick up and sort your letters, then leave while the clerk tidies up.

sections.title: Logging In: USER, PASS and APOP
sections.content:
In the AUTHORIZATION state the client sends USER name and, if the server answers +OK, then PASS string or QUIT. After a good PASS the server takes an exclusive-access lock on the maildrop and splits it into messages numbered 1, 2, and so on. If the lock or the login fails, it answers -ERR and the client may try again.

The password in PASS travels in the clear. Because many clients check mail on a regular schedule, perhaps every five minutes, the risk of capture is higher. The optional APOP name digest command avoids this. The server puts a unique timestamp in its greeting, and the client replies with a 16-octet digest, sent as lower-case hexadecimal, made by applying MD5 to the timestamp (with its angle brackets) followed by a shared secret.

The memo says it is only conjectured that APOP provides origin identification and replay protection. A server that supports both PASS and APOP must not allow both methods for the same user.
sections.eli5: A password in the clear is like shouting your secret across a crowded room. APOP instead mixes your secret with a fresh number the server gave you, so only a scrambled answer is sent.

sections.title: The Command Set
sections.content:
In the TRANSACTION state the client can repeat these commands:

  • STAT gives the number of messages and the total size in octets, not counting those marked deleted.
  • LIST [msg] gives a scan listing: the message number then its size.
  • RETR msg sends the whole message as a multi-line response.
  • DELE msg only marks a message as deleted. Nothing is removed until the UPDATE state.
  • NOOP does nothing and gets a positive reply.
  • LAST returns the highest message number accessed, so a client can infer that higher numbers are unseen.
  • RSET unmarks deleted messages and resets the highest number accessed to zero.

The optional TOP msg n sends the headers, a blank line and the first n lines of the body. The memo strongly discourages extra information in drop and scan listings and prefers optional commands like TOP, so intelligence stays in the client. When the client sends QUIT in TRANSACTION, the server removes the marked messages, releases the lock and closes the connection. A QUIT in AUTHORIZATION just ends the session without an UPDATE state.
sections.eli5: You can count your letters, read one, peek at the top of one, or put a sticker on ones to throw away. The throwing away only happens when you say goodbye.

sections.title: Split User Agents and Security
sections.content:
The memo frames POP3 as part of a split-UA model. The user agent is divided into two functions that talk to the transport system: posting mail with SMTP and retrieving it with POP3. The memo does not specify how a client sends mail, but suggests it connect by SMTP to a relay host, which may or may not be the POP3 server host. A client doing this appears as a user agent and must not be treated as a trusted MTS entity.

The memo also says message transport need not be TCP, using the MZnet project as an example, though it admits MZnet was not fully implemented. Otherwise, apart from the APOP remark, the memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: One helper posts your outgoing letters and a different helper hands you the incoming ones. They are two jobs for the same mail carrier.
